transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), David Park (Redwood SE), Nora Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Carlos Rivera (Blink Head of Platform), Aisha Khan (Blink SRE), Tom Becker (CTO), Meena Patel (Security), Jordan Lee (Dev)

Summary (auto):
- Blink experienced a recurring latency spike under burst load on 2026-03-20; pattern shows p95 spiking to 4.2s for text-gen routes.
- Initial mitigation: routing to a smaller quantized model and temporary increase in dedicated pool size.
- This sync to align on root cause hypotheses, run replays, and define a stability playbook.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, uh we'll try to keep this tight. I know there's some frustration from the weekend incident so we're here to walk through what we saw, next steps, and action items. Carlos, do you want to kick us off with a quick recap?

[00:18] Carlos Rivera: Yeah sure, thanks Maya. So on Friday we had two big spikes, one at 03:10 UTC and another at 04:45 UTC. Both correlated with a marketing blast —heavy short-lived fan-out— and we saw p95 drift from about 600ms to 4.2 seconds. A lot of HTP timeouts downstream, some customer-facing errors.

[00:36] Aisha Khan: And to add, our SLOs were breached for the billing route which is high priority. We did the usual fallback to smaller model but that degraded quality a bit. We opened a ticket with Redwood cause requests for logs and trace artifacts.

[00:52] David Park: Right, we pulled the request traces we have on our side, and there are a couple of signals: big variance in token decode time and some KV cache thrash during the spike window. Key hypothesis is prefix/KV cache invalidation under fan-out leading to extra recomputation in the runtime.

[01:12] Tom Becker: I just want to be clear — is this an infra autoscale delay or something in the model serving that makes token loops slow? Feels like both.

[01:21] David Park: Yeah, it's a combination. Autoscale reacted but with some lag for the particular pod group. And the runtime's kernel selection when sequence lengths changed rapidly sometimes picked a less optimal kernel path; that plus cache misses increases per-token CPU/GPU time.

[01:41] Jordan Lee: Sorry, David, when you say cache misses do you mean the KV cache or a local LRU? We saw KV hit rates drop in the logs.

[01:48] David Park: KV cache, yeah. There's prefix caching for common prompt prefixes; that was being evicted under the burst pattern. Also the KV cache snapshot we have is partial — our log sampling didn't capture the full window. We need the kernel traces to confirm the kernel switch events.

[02:08] Meena Patel: From security, we need to make sure shared traces don't include PII. Carlos, can you confirm export policy?

[02:15] Carlos Rivera: We'll scrub PII. We can create a staging-access token with role-limited access.

[02:22] Maya Chen: Great, thanks. On the mitigation side we proposed two things in the interim: route high-volume short requests to a quantized v2 model and bump dedicated capacity for weekend windows. Both seemed to reduce p95 in the immediate mitigation.

[02:41] Aisha Khan: The quality hit from the quantized v2 is acceptable for user flows that are tolerant, but billing route fails a little too often. We need more surgical fixes.

[02:51] David Park: Agreed. Surgical fixes we discussed: prefix cache guardrails (prevent eviction of hot prefixes during fan-out), tweak autoscaler thresholds for burst patterns, and force kernel pinning for sequences between 64–128 tokens to avoid suboptimal kernel fallbacks.

[03:14] Tom Becker: Kernel pinning — will that require a restart? How disruptive?

[03:20] David Park: It can be applied as a rolling config flag with no major downtime; it will bias kernel selection but we need to validate on staging. We'll provide the commands and a canary plan.

[03:33] Carlos Rivera: Can Redwood run a controlled replay? We want to run it on our staging but may need your help to interpret results.

[03:38] David Park: Yes. We'll provide a replay harness and a script to replay the exact request trace. Two notes: A) replay should be run with and without prefix cache to prove delta, B) we need the kernel-level trace and the KV cache snapshot from your side.

[03:58] Aisha Khan: We can provide the traces but need instructions for the sanitization step. Meena, any security constraints?

[04:05] Meena Patel: We require PII redaction and an audit log of who accessed the artifacts. If Redwood needs staging access, it'll be via a temporary role and we'll log every action.

[04:16] Nora Alvarez: We'll coordinate the access flow. Maya, I'll follow up with the doc template for redaction.

[04:24] Maya Chen: Cool. Also wanted to call out something we noticed in the runtime logs — during the spike there's a sudden increase in the 'token decode' CPU usage which aligns with kernel selection jitter. That suggests a model-engine/runtime interplay not just infra.

[04:40] Jordan Lee: Is it possible the model variant selection logic is flapping between full precision and quantized paths when memory pressure changes?

[04:47] David Park: Yes, that's plausible—our runtime has heuristics that try to pick a quantized exec path when memory is constrained but under rapid changes it can oscillate. We're going to add hysteresis to those heuristics in the short term.

[05:02] Tom Becker: OK. For our incident review, we need a timeline written for execs and a technical appendix for SREs. Who owns the timeline?

[05:11] Maya Chen: Redwood will draft the timeline and include the traces we have. Blink to add their request logs and sanitize. Nora will combine into a single artifact.

[05:20] Carlos Rivera: Fine. Also, is there a recommendation for backup routing? We had a long-tail problem where fallback to smaller model created quality regressions; maybe better to degrade feature-set instead of model.

[05:32] David Park: Absolutely, feature gating is a great tactical option—turn off non-critical enrichment or do token budget enforcement before switching models. We'll add that to the playbook.

[05:44] Aisha Khan: About autoscale: our current policy scales based on CPU per pod and overall queue length. We saw pods spin up but new pods took ~18s to become ready. Can Redwood help tune warm pool thresholds?

[05:57] David Park: Yes, warm pools + pre-warming a small percentage of replicas reduces cold-start latency. We'll propose a policy: maintain a 10% warm pool during known marketing windows and a burst pool that can be borrowed. We'll include sample HPA (or equivalent) config.

[06:14] Meena Patel: Security question — do we need to enable private deployment for this use case? Does Private deployment materially change the kernel/serving behavior?

[06:23] Maya Chen: Private gives you more control over networking and KMS options but runtime is mostly same; however, Private deployments can give you direct access to kernel-level logs and the ability to run custom builds. We can discuss a pilot.

[06:35] Tom Becker: Cost question — how much does dedicated pool increase cost for weekends?

[06:40] Maya Chen: We'll send a weekend bump estimate. Quick ballpark — depends on instance type, but we'll quantify in the pricing follow-up.

[06:49] Carlos Rivera: What's the immediate observable we should watch during the replay? p50, p95, kernel switch count, KV hit rate?

[06:57] David Park: Exactly those plus GPU utilization and encoder/decoder times. We'll provide a template dashboard capture.

[07:07] Nora Alvarez: I'll attach the replay harness and log-sanitization instructions to the follow-up. Also will note the audit requirements from Meena.

[07:15] Maya Chen: OK let's talk about the stability playbook steps and run cadence. Immediate (1 week): run replays, collect traces, and run small canary of kernel pinning in staging. Medium (2–3 weeks): add prefix cache guardrails and warm pool config; schedule weekend pilot. Long-term: consider dedicated routing for billing route and a private deployment pilot if you need kernel-level observability.

[07:45] Aisha Khan: That sounds reasonable. Who will own the canary run?

[07:50] David Park: Redwood SE will run the canary together with Blink SRE. We'll need temporary staging access.

[07:56] Tom Becker: Let's make sure the Exec timeline is ready by Tuesday for our leadership meeting.

[08:02] Maya Chen: Yep we'll target Tuesday. Nora will own the doc merge.

[08:07] Carlos Rivera: One more thing — we saw one pod emitting repeated "failed to allocate KV buffer" logs. Could that be a memory leak?

[08:15] David Park: Could be, or it could be a transient OOM triggered by a pathological request. We'll correlate with kernel traces and GPU memory metrics. If it's a leak, we'll escalate to the runtime team.

[08:27] Jordan Lee: If it's a leak and requires patching, what's the expected turnaround?

[08:31] Maya Chen: We'll triage within 48 hours; if a code patch is required, typical SLAs are 1–2 weeks depending on severity. We'll keep Blink posted.

[08:40] Meena Patel: For now, any artifacts you share with us need to have an access log and limited retention. 30 days retention for traces is fine.

[08:48] Nora Alvarez: Noted.

[08:51] Maya Chen: Alright let's recap next steps: Redwood provides kernel-level traces, replay harness, and a canary plan; Blink provides sanitized request logs and grants staging access; both run replay and share results. We'll meet next week after initial replays.

[09:05] Tom Becker: Good. Thanks everyone.

[09:09] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up in email and post the docs to the shared folder.
